Business.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
Business.text:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claims

McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'

Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuse

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

Business.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
Business.text:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.

But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."

Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.

Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.

Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.

And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

Business.title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
Business.text:
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.

Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.

Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.

Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.

The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.

The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".

The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.

The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.

In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

Business.title: Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
Business.text:
Anthropic closed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17% higher than its initial public offering price. At the close of market on Thursday, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn total market capitalization, $1.75tn fully diluted.

While the final share value was higher than the IPO price of $83, it marked a dip from an early high of $111.50. The firm’s shares initially soared 34% when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn. Nonetheless, Anthropic’s ranked among the biggest stock market flotations in history. The artificial intelligence startup, founded in 2021, became one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” said Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, who rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Anthropic announced late on Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters, an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June.

US stocks slumped at the end of trading, a potential sign that Anthropic’s mammoth IPO wasn’t enough to alleviate concerns over the AI industry’s volatility. Most of the major chipmakers’ stock prices closed the day lower than they started. While Nvidia hit its sixth day of losses after its latest earnings call, other players like Micron and Broadcom also saw their share prices decline.

The company’s listing serves as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry are watching closely how it fares on the public market.

Anthropic’s stock market debut makes it the first firm focused entirely on AI “uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business” to be publicly traded, analysts at Yorkville Ives said.

“Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a memo.

The company has seen explosive growth in revenue every year of its existence – sometimes more than 1,000% – according to its investor prospectus, filed at the end of October. Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.

“You’ve seen an astronomical growth rate in terms of the top line,” said Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm. “The question investors are going to be looking at leading up to the IPO, and once it’s public, is what happens to that growth rate.”

Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm expects its costs to balloon as it works to secure more compute, which refers to the processing and computational power provided by arrays of semiconductor chips often located in datacenters. It is the resource that powers generative artificial intelligence and Anthropic’s single largest expense, about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026.

“The development of frontier AI models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars,” the company’s executives wrote in the prospectus.

Anthropic has disclosed in great detail all the ways its AI models may pose a danger to humanity – including being used to develop bioweapons or deepen repression around the world. Amodei has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that the companies were building them irresponsibility.

The company beat competitors like OpenAI to launching on the US stock market. However, the IPO comes amid uncertainty as the industry braces for any additional impact or fallout from the recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang.

There is “huge volatility in the market”, and investors are going to be looking at how sustainable the company’s AI growth is, said Schlossman. Investors are also keen to see how important Anthropic will be in the larger AI ecosystem. The company has focused primarily on enterprise customers rather than individual consumers. Anthropic’s Claude code product has proved popular with software engineers.

Business.title: US ⁠judge allows Trump’s $15bn lawsuit against New York Times to proceed
Business.text:
A federal ⁠judge in Florida on Thursday said Donald Trump’s $15bn defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory ⁠for the US president in his ⁠legal campaign ​against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.

US district judge Steven Merryday in Tampa dismissed two claims in the suit while allowing core defamation claims to move forward.

The president’s claim against the publishers alleges defamation by three New York Times reporters – Susanne Craig, Russ Buettner and Peter Baker – in two articles published by the outlet and a 2024 book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success, which was co-authored by Craig and Buettner.

Trump claims the articles and book contain false statements that damaged his businesses and personal reputation. An earlier, 80-page version of the complaint was thrown out because it did not contain a concise summary and was filled with “vituperation and invective”, the court said.

An amended, 40-page complaint was filed in October last year that removed references to the 2024 presidential election. Mediation talks failed, along with a request by the defendants to move the action to federal court in New York.

The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.

In dismissing two of Trump’s claims, Merryday, an appointee of George HW Bush, said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing ​Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.

In his claim, Trump cited 22 statements from a ⁠book by Baker and 12 from the articles ​by Craig and Buettner. They include assertions about Trump’s role in ​creating his hit reality ‌TV show The Apprentice, ​his inheritance from ​his father, his business ventures, and his upbringing in New York.

Representatives for the New York Times and Penguin Random House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesperson for the Times, has previously said “the lawsuit remains obviously meritless”. A spokesperson for Penguin Random House has also described the action as “meritless” and said it “stands by the book and its authors”.

Reuters contributed reporting

Business.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
Business.text:
Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees.

Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown.

In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday.

Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter.

“We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.”

When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”.

When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”.

Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions.

Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”.

Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.”

Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”.

“While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.”

Business.title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
Business.text:
Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.

Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.

According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.

“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”

The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.

While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.

In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.

Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

Business.title: Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim
Business.text:
Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.

A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.

The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”

However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.

Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.

The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.

Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said.

Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.

The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.

The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.

Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.

“We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”

The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”

“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino: Man Utd boss priorities include Fernandes, culture and defence
Sports.text:
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

There is a clear non-negotiable.

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

Then there is Dalot.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.

United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than £1.1bn and a further £14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.

This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.

"We need to be united," said Pochettino.

"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

Sports.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: George Russell fastest in second practice after rain
Sports.text:
Mercedes driver George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.

Russell, competing with Red Bull's Max Verstappen for second in the championship in the final three races of the year, set his time right at the end of the session.

The same applied to Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who went second, 0.071 seconds behind Russell, with a lap even later the Briton's.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, the main pace-setter throughout the session, was third fastest ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

The Frenchman had a faster lap ruined when he was blocked by Haas' Oliver Bearman at the end of the Strip.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth, ahead of of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and the second McLaren of Lando Norris, who was fastest in the wettest early part of the session.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.

Piastri will have a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance this season.

The new internal combustion engine the Australian needs as a result of a failure at the Mexico City Grand Prix two races ago is his fifth of the season - only four are permitted.

Piastri and team-mate Norris will also use the latest turbo Mercedes have produced under F1's engine upgrade scheme but that comes penalty-free.

That is not the case for Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will take the new turbo but it is his fifth of the season, so he also has a 10-place penalty which team-mate Alex Albon avoids despite also fitting the new turbo.

At the factory team, only Antonelli will use the new turbo. The team decided it was not worth Russell having it as it would have given him a 15-place grid penalty.

The turbo provides only a small performance upgrade and is more aimed at expanding the engine's useability for the 2027 season.

Bearman also has a grid penalty for engine changes and is set to start from the back of the grid.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino: New manager's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
Sports.text:
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."

Manchester United have declined to comment.

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

Sports.title: Arsenal 0-2 Lyon: French side show Gunners bridge to gap
Sports.text:
It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.

That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.

In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.

Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.

On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.

One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.

Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.

In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.

Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.

Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.

Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.

"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers said.

"They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances."

Lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.

Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.

Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.

As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.

Slegers also said Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.

Asked how far off Lyon they currently are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.

"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.

"But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us."

Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.

They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.

"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.

"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period."

It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.

Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.

They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.

Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.

Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.

Giraldez said time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.

"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.

"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.

"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season."

Sports.title: Grand Slam of Darts 2026: Luke Humphries upset by unseeded Tom Sykes in second round
Sports.text:
Luke Humphries followed Luke Littler in exiting the Grand Slam of Darts after losing 10-9 to unseeded Tom Sykes in a second-round thriller.

Having trailed 4-0 and 9-7, the second seed battled back to force a deciding leg and had the advantage of throwing first.

But his fellow Englishman Sykes was unfazed, quickly took control of the leg and when Humphries missed double 10 for a 128 checkout to snatch victory, the world number 81 nervelessly hit double 18 to secure a place in his first major quarter-final.

"It's unbelievable," Sykes, 34, told Sky Sports. "Luke let me off a few times in the first bit but I set off really well.

"When he got it back to 5-5, I thought 'here we go' and he started turning it on in the last 10 legs, but I'm just buzzing to get over the line.

"I was a bit nervous [going for double 18 for the match]. I thought the game was over when I saw Luke hit the the first treble 18, then the second.

"But I was so cold on that last one, I thought 'just hit it first dart, no messing about' and I did. I'm riding a wave at the minute and I'll keep trying to ride it."

Sykes' victory was all the more impressive given Humphries did not play badly at all, averaging 102.02 and hitting 37% on the doubles.

But the Castleford thrower made a flying start, averaging just shy of 108 in the first mini-session, to earn a sizeable lead and maintained his composure as the former world champion fought back.

He will face three-time Grand Slam champion Michael van Gerwen in the last eight after the Dutchman beat seventh seed James Wade 10-8.

In a high-class contest that saw six 100-plus finishes, Wade earned a 7-5 lead but Van Gerwen, who finished with an average of 103.83, took out 121 to level at 7-7.

He broke again to go 9-7 up and although Wade hit a 130 checkout to break back, 10th seed Van Gerwen made it three breaks in a row to avoid a one-leg shootout.

With Humphries and Littler gone, third seed Gian van Veen is the top-ranked player remaining in the draw in Wolverhampton.

The Dutchman beat Germany's Martin Schindler 10-7 and was completely dominant before a slight wobble as he tried to close out the win.

Van Veen raced into a 9-3 lead but then proceeded to lose four legs on the spin, missing three match darts, before eventually finishing the job.

England's Nathan Aspinall awaits last year's World Championship finalist in the quarters after a 10-7 win over German Gabriel Clemens.

'The Asp' averaged 100.72 and posted an impressive 53% checkout rate as he came out on top in a back-and-forth match.

Sports.title: Sandpapergate: Pat Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew
Sports.text:
Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.

The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.

It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.

Therefore, this day of reckoning was always going to come.

Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.

Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.

Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.

But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.

Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.

In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.

Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.

I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.

Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.

Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.

The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.

Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.

After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.

He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.

Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.

The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.

If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.

Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.

And what about next summer's Ashes? If Cummins is tossing the coin at Trent Bridge on 18 June, then he is extraordinarily resilient.

Right now, I can't imagine that happening. He has said he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, which is ludicrous when you think what he will face on that tour: scrutiny from the media, constant baiting from the crowds.

Cummins will have to decide if he has the stomach for all of that, and whether he can see it through.

His way out could be to resign, without admitting guilt. To say the speculation has become a distraction for the team and the pressure is taking a toll on his family life – we have seen more pictures from Australia overnight of Cummins being confronted outside his home.

Cummins could perhaps continue in the ranks, just as Warner and Smith did. A resignation without an admission of guilt may also take the heat off the other bowlers – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.

Whether Cummins continues or not, questions will remain for others who were in Cape Town, Cricket Australia and the whole culture of the sport in that country.

Looking now at what happened in 2018, it appears there was an attitude in the Australia camp that they were fireproof, that they could get away with anything.

Credit goes to their media manager Kate Hutchison, who, according to Bancroft, made a stand about what was going on and knew what would happen if and when the Aussies got caught.

What about the others involved, coaches who were supposed to guide and protect young men? Darren Lehmann and his position at Northamptonshire, or David Saker, who has recently been working with England.

Cricket Australia has seemed so reluctant to get involved. If the big idea was to give individuals the opportunity to "tell their truth" behind closed doors, it is surely dead in the water.

What about telling THE truth? Nothing else is good enough.

Sports.title: Mykhailo Mudryk: Andriy Shevchenko disputes player's doping claims
Sports.text:
Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.

Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.

In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.

He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.

"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."

He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.

In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.

And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".

"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.

"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.

"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."

BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

Sports.title: England: Football Association punished by Uefa after fans' anti-Catholic chants against Spain in Nations League
Sports.text:
England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

Sports.title: England vs New Zealand: Maro Itoje says mood in camp has changed
Sports.text:
Captain Maro Itoje says a clearer sense of purpose and unity has coincided with improved performances from England this autumn.

They have won their last four games, racking up victories over Fiji, Argentina, Australia and Japan in the Nations Championship.

Prior to that run, England had lost five successive Tests - a streak that included their worst ever Six Nations campaign.

They host New Zealand on Saturday, with the All Blacks stung by their first defeat by Wales in 73 years last time out.

"It feels a lot more cohesive," Itoje told BBC Rugby Union Weekly.

"It feels, from a player's point of view, that our understanding of what we're trying to do is a lot clearer.

"The level of understanding has grown from campaign to campaign and we have a very clear sense of what we're doing, what we're trying to do and we're getting into those positions a lot more effectively now."

A Times report earlier this month, external claimed senior players had sought a summit meeting with head coach Steve Borthwick after their July Nations Championship campaign due to differences of opinion over the team's direction.

Itoje was rested for that tour and Jamie George, who had reassumed the captaincy in his absence, said parts of the article were untrue and the squad were "incredibly disappointed" by its publication.

"As senior players part of our job is to challenge Steve," said George at the time. "Steve is so open to us giving feedback and having challenge."

In turn, Borthwick has credited his senior players with leading a drive on discipline that has helped England's results turn a corner.

Across their first eight Tests in 2026, England were shown 14 yellow cards and a red.

It was highlighted as a key area to improve before the autumn and they have responded with no cards and only 15 penalties conceded across their two November Tests so far.

"It's never just one thing, but I will talk about one matter," added Borthwick of the reasons behind the improvement.

"A number of weeks ago, the senior players led the players in groups. It was a big discussion topic and coming out it was a series of commitments that the players made about what they need to do.

"They've backed up those commitments in this first couple weeks. Now we know that's going be tested even more this weekend."

Sports.title: ATP Finals: Alexander Zverev beats Arthur Fils to put Ben Shelton through to semi-finals
Sports.text:
World number one Alexander Zverev said he would do "everything I can to be pain-free" after hurting his ankle during his ATP Finals victory over Arthur Fils.

Germany's Zverev ensured he finished top of the John McEnroe Group with a 6-4 7-6 (8-6) win over Fils - a result which also sent Ben Shelton through to the semi-finals.

However, the French and US Open champion's serve speeds dropped throughout the match and he repeatedly gestured and grimaced.

Zverev said afterwards he felt pain in his right ankle - the same place where he tore ligaments in a career-threatening injury in 2022.

"It's a tendon that goes over my bone, and it moved when I broke my ankle," the 29-year-old explained.

"The ankle is a topic that probably will stay until the end of my career.

"I'm going to do everything I can to be pain-free on Saturday, but this is something I have to live with nowadays.

"I can still move well, but you can see immediately my serve speeds go down. I hope I'll be 100% on Saturday."

US Open runner-up Shelton needed Zverev to beat Fils to be assured of a place in the semi-finals.

The American earlier had to fight for just over two hours to beat fast-rising Spaniard Rafael Jodar 7-6 (10-8) 7-5.

Zverev will play either Daniil Medvedev or Frances Tiafoe in Saturday's semi-finals, while Shelton will face Carlos Alcaraz.

Seven-time major champion Alcaraz practised on Thursday after having a scan on "a little problem" in his hamstring that he picked up during his win over Medvedev.

Zverev will hope to brush off his own injury concerns as he bids to win the tournament for a third time.

He has yet to lose a set in Turin or have his serve broken, and his match against Fils mirrored his previous wins over Shelton and Jodar.

After a strong start, Fils played an error-strewn game at 3-3 in the first set to hand the initiative to his opponent.

With such a huge first serve Zverev is one of the most difficult players to break, and he kept Fils at bay before serving out the opener in one minute flat.

In the second set Fils played a superb return game at 6-5 to force two break points on the Zverev serve, but they were calmly saved by the top seed.

Zverev led the tie-break 6-1 but, distracted by his ankle and a re-energised Fils, five match points went by before he finally closed out victory.

Sports.title: LPGA Tour: England's Charley Hull one stroke off lead at lucrative season finale
Sports.text:
CME Group Tour Championship - round one leaderboard

-7 K Davidson (Aus), AL Kim (Kor), J Thitikul (Tha); -6 C Hull (Eng

Selected others: -6 L Coughlin (US), A Kim (US), P Roussin-Bouchard (Fra); -5 Y Noh (US), L Woad (Eng), G Lopez (Mex), C Boutier (Fra) -4 N Korda (US), C Ciganda (Spa); -2 L Maguire (Ire)

England's Charley Hull carded a six-under-par 66 to sit one shot off the first-round lead at the LPGA's lucrative season-ending CME Group Tour Championship.

Australia's Karis Davidson, South Korea's Kim A-lim and Thailand's Jeeno Thitikul, set the pace at seven under at the Tiburon Golf Club in Naples, Florida.

World number two Thitikul, who is aiming to win the event for the third consecutive season, responded to a bogey on the 12th hole by knocking in five consecutive birdies on the back nine.

Hull, who triumphed a decade ago, is one of nine players a stroke behind the leading trio on a stacked leaderboard that contains the top 60 in this season's points list, who are all chasing the $4m (£3.05m) top prize.

"When I won 10 years ago I didn't really take golf seriously. I remember coming into this event when I won, hungover," Hull said.

"I felt pretty good [today]. I kind of like lost my swing feels [at the] end of last week because my hip was very tight, and it just like started rerouting my golf swing," Hull said.

"Today I was nervous on the first tee. I felt like I had no swing feeling. Then as the round developed I felt like I hit it really nice."

Hull's compatriot Lottie Woad made six birdies and a bogey as she signed for five-under 67, along with France's Celine Boutier.

World number one Nelly Korda, who will qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame if she wins on Sunday, endured a mixed day but picked up shots on the 17th and 18th as she finished on four under.

With an $11m purse on offer, Korda would also break Annika Sorenstam's career earnings record if she finishes in sixth place or better.

The Swede amassed 10 major titles and earned $22,583,694 during a storied career before retiring in 2008, with Korda now just under $160,000 behind that mark.

Gaming_Tech.title: Thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret operation
Gaming_Tech.text:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted

On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted

On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

Gaming_Tech.title: GTA 6 breaks records as estimated sales top $2.3bn
Gaming_Tech.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.

The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas.

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.

Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.

Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.

The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.

If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
Gaming_Tech.text:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.

At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.
