TechnologyTab.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
TechnologyTab.text:
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas, 59.

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.

The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".

In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.

In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

As it heeled over, five people were injured, either by falling or by items falling on them and a deckhand was thrown into the sea, the report said.

As water started entering the yacht, two of the guests "used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder to exit into the central alleyway", then climbed along the internal walls to get into the saloon.

TechnologyTab.title: Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
TechnologyTab.text:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.

Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.

The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.

Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.

He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.

"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.

In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.

Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.

The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.

Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.

Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

TechnologyTab.title: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises
TechnologyTab.text:
The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.

While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.

The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.

Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.

It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.

The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.

Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.

Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.

The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.

But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.

AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.

It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.

One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.

The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.

And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.

It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.

Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.

It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.

TechnologyTab.title: UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
TechnologyTab.text:
After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews., external

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.

GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.

Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating, external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".

One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.

The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.

The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".

It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.

"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.

Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.

Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".

About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".

Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.

"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald, external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.

"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.

"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".

Players were able to download the 212GB game ahead of time, in order to be able to play it as soon as it was made available.

Some had even gone to the lengths of buying a whole new console dedicated to the game.

Broadband providers Virgin Media O2, as well as BT and EE, said internet traffic records had been broken in the days leading up to the UK release.

The BBC has heard from people planning to take time off work - as well as a company which has given its employees the day off - in order to dedicate time to the game.

Kieran Youens-Byrne, 34, from Manchester said he was "going on a pilgrimage to Wales" where he would be "completely off grid" for a week.

He added his partner Clare "has been incredibly understanding, although I suspect she's questioning why our romantic getaway revolves around a PlayStation".

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average...

TechnologyTab.title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
TechnologyTab.text:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".

And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.

"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".

Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".

The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.

"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.

"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."

Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

TechnologyTab.title: Hacks, AI or overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
TechnologyTab.text:
Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks, as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language.

These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.

There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.

As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.

A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.

It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.

Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.

Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.

But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.

AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.

And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.

Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.

Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.

"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.

In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.

This happened in the recent Java incident, as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.

Then there are the outages.

These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.

Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.

A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.

With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.

Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.

In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.

"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."

In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.

At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose.

Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.

Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.

They also shine a light on the world's heavy reliance on a small number of players.

Not just frontier AI companies, but infrastructure providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, which - along with Google - run a huge chunk of the world's computer servers.

In the PHP incident, the world was holding its breath as one programmer - working voluntarily - worked to issue patches in a form that was easily applicable.

And Java, run by another tech giant Oracle, is used by nearly all of the biggest companies on Earth.

"The Oracle Java vulnerability is a stark reminder of how dependent businesses have become on a relatively small number of critical technologies," said Sheila Pancholi, risk assurance lead at consultancy firm RSM UK.

"Organisations need to know where their critical technology dependencies sit, act quickly when vulnerabilities emerge, and test that their response has actually worked."

Meanwhile Xander Van Raemdonck, security engineer at Aikido Security, said the challenge was "knowing whether you're exposed".

"Java is bundled inside a huge amount of business software, so many companies don't have a full list of where it runs," he said.

Perhaps for now.

The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades.

"AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness.

"So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."

Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions.

Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated.

Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks.

"Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said.

"We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."

The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

TechnologyTab.title: PM urges social media companies to 'show some decency' and take down Brand video
TechnologyTab.text:
Social media companies should "show some decency and take these videos down", the prime minister has said, following a government attempt to have a YouTube video featuring a message from the jailed comedian removed.

The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Speaking following a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Andy Burnham said it was "time that we focus on the victims and think about them," rather than "hearing from a convicted criminal".

He said: "I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. Why are we having to hear from him. We shouldn't be and certainly [victims] shouldn't be hearing from him."

But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.

"Show some decency and take these videos down."

Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Laura Brand shared a video on their Sunday Service channel on the website and read out a message from her husband in which he said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be removed, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.

"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."

However, the BBC understands there are no new plans to update or bring fresh legislation governing online platforms as a result of Brand's case.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".

Badenoch told Today, YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".

"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.

Connie Shaw of the Free Speech Union backed Badenoch's comments, saying that "if we want to protect everyone's free speech, we have to protect the free speech of even the most heinous people".

Speaking to the BBC's Politics Live, she said that it would "set a very dangerous precedent if we said that Russell Brand's wife is not able to express the fact that he rejects the fact that he has been found guilty".

Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".

Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.

In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.

"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."

The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.

Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.

"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

Additional reporting by Steven McIntosh and political correspondent Harry Farley

TechnologyTab.title: Labor leaders call on governments to stop awarding Amazon public contracts
TechnologyTab.text:
More than 30 labor union leaders from 19 countries are calling on governments to review their public contracts with Amazon and Amazon Web Services, citing the company’s poor record on worker rights and collective bargaining, in an open letter published on Thursday.

“Amazon’s consistent record of disrespect for workers’ fundamental rights should disqualify it from being awarded public contracts – its behaviour is fundamentally inconsistent with the shared democratic values of our countries,” the union leaders wrote.

The letter cites Amazon’s anti-union activity around the world, including over a decade of strikes by workers in Germany, its decision to shut down its Quebec warehouses after a warehouse voted to unionize in 2024, allegations of retaliating and silencing workers in Australia and legally challenging labor laws in the US and Canada.

In the US, the Institute for Local Self Reliance estimates cities, counties and school districts spent $2.2bn on Amazon in 2023.

Amazon has also secured several multibillion-dollar contracts with the US federal government in recent years, including a nearly $2.6bn award from the Department of Homeland Security in 2026 and a 10-year contract with the National Security Agency that was renewed in 2022, reportedly worth up to $10bn.

“Our governments continue to award Amazon billions in public contracts for cloud computing services underpinning critical public infrastructure,” the leaders wrote. “This pattern reveals a dangerous disconnect between public procurement practices and the democratic values our societies are meant to uphold, while creating unnecessary risks for public services.”

Signers from the US include Stuart Appelbaum, president of the Retail Wholesale Department Store Union (RWDSU); Milton Jones, international president of the United Food and Commercial Workers; Claude Cummings Jr, president of Communications Workers of America; Sean O’Brien, president of the Teamsters; April Verrett, president of the Service Employees International Union (SEIU); and Jonathan Smith, president of the American Postal Workers Union.

Christy Hoffman, general secretary of UNI Global Union; Lana Payne, national president of Canadian trade union Unifor; Gary Smith, general secretary of the UK’s GMB; and Frank Werneke, president of ver.di in Germany also signed the letter.

“Every public contract is a choice about what governments are willing to pay for. Right now, taxpayers in country after country are paying Amazon while it shuts down warehouses, busts unions and tries to get labour laws struck down,” Hoffman said in a statement. “Governments set the rules for who gets public money. They can require that companies respect workers’ right to organize and bargain, and they should start with the biggest contractor that refuses to.”

The letter comes as the UK Home Office is planning to renew its Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud computing contract for a possible cost of £881.6m over two years.

Governments could reform public procurement rules to make certain worker rights standards mandatory for contractors along with establishing enforcement mechanisms that would exclude corporations that violate workers’ rights from future public contracts.

“Public funds should advance public values, not subsidize union busting or deepen our digital dependency on unaccountable corporate power,” the letter concludes.

A spokesperson for Amazon disputed the letter.

“This group is being intentionally misleading and continues to promote a false narrative. The fact is at Amazon we provide great pay, great benefits, and great opportunities – all from day one,” the spokesperson said in an email. “We directly employ more than 1.5 million people around the world, and provide a modern, safe, and engaging workplace whether you work in an office or at one of our operations buildings.”

TechnologyTab.title: Democrats demand answers from Howard Lutnick about Nvidia and his family’s business
TechnologyTab.text:
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, faces mounting questions over his handling of the Nvidia affair as Democratic lawmakers demand answers over his family firm’s vast stake in the tech company.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration, held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees.

“The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.

Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.

But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia.

They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.

Raskin is the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives. Meeks is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Kamlager-Dove is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs subcommittee on south and central Asia.

In an accompanying news release, the lawmakers said that they were seeking to determine whether Lutnick “blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock”.

Howard Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald until his confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025, when he transferred his stake in the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children.

In the letter to Brandon Lutnick, the lawmakers wrote that at the time of Howard Lutnick’s confirmation, Cantor Fitzgerald had “amassed a significant stake” in Nvidia, reportedly “holding more than 3.5m shares, valued at over $1.3bn”.

In a statement to the Guardian, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said that the claims in the letter were “inaccurate”. “Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” the spokesperson said. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients.

“The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position,” the statement continued. “Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless. Additionally, Cantor has no role in US export control or entity list decisions [to determine trade restrictions].”

The Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson also said that they were “confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations”.

In their letter, the lawmakers also cited a recent New York Times report that Howard Lutnick had pushed to weaken rules affecting south-east Asian datacenters, some of which are Cantor Fitzgerald clients.

A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the US and that he does not discuss department matters with his sons. The spokesperson added that Lutnick’s sons also do not discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him.

In their letter on Tuesday, the lawmakers asked Cantor Fitzgerald to provide written confirmation that it had “implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records” by 5pm ET on 1 December.

The letter comes after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, following reports of his multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The developments have put Lutnick into focus as last week Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.

EntertainmentTab.title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs with Keith Urban
EntertainmentTab.text:
US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.

The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history.

"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."

Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."

Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.

She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.

Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.

Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.

"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.

"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."

Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.

Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.

Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.

The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.

Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

EntertainmentTab.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
EntertainmentTab.text:
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.

The actress wrote on Instagram, external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".

"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"

She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."

In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."

Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.

In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".

"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."

She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.

"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.

"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

EntertainmentTab.title: Fiona Harvey, who allegedly inspired Baby Reindeer, to appear at Crown Court on harassment charge
EntertainmentTab.text:
A woman who allegedly inspired the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix drama Baby Reindeer is to appear at Harrow Crown Court on charges of racially aggravated harassment without violence.

Fiona Harvey, 61, is accused of sending several emails and three voicemails including antisemitic material to lawyer Mark Lewis, between 4 September and 9 October 2025.

During a hearing at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday, the court heard that Lewis initially believed Harvey was a potential client.

Harvey of Camden, north London, did not indicate a plea, but elected for a Crown Court trial.

The charge is an either-way offence, which means it can be heard in either a magistrates' court or Crown Court.

She will next appear at Harrow Crown Court for a pre-trial preparation hearing on 17 December.

Harvey has previously identified herself as the woman on whom Martha is based, after the release of Richard Gadd's Emmy Award-winning series in 2024.

She is suing the streamer £128m for defamation, negligence and privacy violations, arguing that that Netflix told "brutal lies" about her to over 50 million viewers around the world.

Netflix denies the claim, which will be heard in front of a jury on May 18, 2027, at the US District Court for the Central District of California.

EntertainmentTab.title: Rob Brydon says he invented his own fake agent to negotiate fees
EntertainmentTab.text:
Rob Brydon has revealed he pretended to be his own agent at the start of his career when he was working as a TV and radio presenter in Wales.

The actor, best known for playing Stacey's Uncle Bryn in the hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, told BBC One's Graham Norton Show, external he used to step into the role of his fake agent to arrange bookings for events.

"I would get asked to go and do things, and I didn't really have an agent at that time so I invented a guy called Richard Knight," Brydon told the show.

The fictional agent would phone organisers and negotiate a fee for Brydon's appearance, he said.

The actor, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, shared an anecdote about being invited to a fundraiser and managing to get a fee for it.

"I'm terribly embarrassed," he told the show's host and fellow guests Cynthia Erivo, David Tennant and Laura Linney.

"They were all there for the good of their hearts," he said.

Brydon, known for his ability to mimic a range of celebrities, went on to impersonate the fictional Richard Knight asking for money in return for an appearance, with the agent describing Brydon as "an angel".

"I would go to these events and they would say 'oh I spoke to Mr Knight, he's quite a character', and I would say 'more than you realise'," Brydon told the show.

The 61-year-old actor stars in new sitcom Bill's Included in which he plays Bill Beam, a divorced man who rents his spare rooms to four students to stay financially afloat while "trying his very best to be their friend".

He told the Press Association he was drawn to his latest comedy role because he had missed acting in sitcoms since featuring in Gavin and Stacey.

The popular show ended in January 2010, although Christmas specials aired in 2019 and 2024.

While Brydon has since hosted shows including Destination X and Would I Lie To You?, the new show marks his return to the sitcom format.

"He calls himself a land-friend, not a landlord," Brydon said of his character Bill Beam.

EntertainmentTab.title: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
EntertainmentTab.text:
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).

The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.

The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.

It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it in 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Westside Cowboy named BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026
EntertainmentTab.text:
Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.

Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.

The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.

Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".

BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK, providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.

About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.

Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.

The four-piece played in various other bands before coming together to form Westside Cowboy.

Haycocks, O'Connell, and Murphy had met at Manchester's Royal Northern College of Music in 2021 and later got to know Bradbury after meeting him in the nearby Johnny Roadhouse music shop.

Murphy and Bradbury played in surf-rock trio Katz, while Murphy and Haycocks both worked together in noise-pop trio, DieKaiDie, but it was when Bradbury, who was working in the music shop repairing guitars, asked the others if they wanted to start a new band that Westside Cowboy's journey began.

He said the band's obvious camaraderie was one of their main selling points.

"They're still the same four mates wandering down Oxford Road in Manchester, and the reason the music has resonated with so many people is because it's a true reflection of those four kids," he said.

"They've been themselves and, in doing so, have brought the fashion and style of the past 10 years of UK post-punk culture down to earth."

EntertainmentTab.title: Glastonbury 2027 line-up: Harry Styles, Cher, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish to headline
EntertainmentTab.text:
Harry Styles will make his Glastonbury festival debut next year as one of the event's headliners, alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish - with Cher among the other stars on the bill.

The veteran US pop icon will play the coveted Sunday afternoon "legends" slot, which is often considered a fourth headline set. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.

Other acts on the line-up include Sombr, Sienna Spiro, Lily Allen, The Streets, Chase & Status, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream and breakout pop star Adéla.

Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes last month, with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.

Electro pioneers Kraftwerk will make their Glastonbury debut with a headline set at West Holts - the festival's third-largest stage.

The event will also welcome experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine, who have drawn attention for their prog-rock sound and polka-dotted stage costumes; rap legends De La Soul and Mike D; and pop provocateur FKA Twigs.

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.

"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"

The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.

Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.

Sam Fender will headline the first night, in what will be his second appearance at the festival.

He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.

"Me and the boys have never been here before," he said. "We've never been here as punters, never played here before and we're doing that all in one day, which is the most crazy experience."

He will return as one of the UK's biggest rock stars, having won the Mercury Prize for his third album, People Watching, in 2025. Earlier this year, his duet with Olivia Dean - Rein Me In - became the UK's longest-running number one single of all time.

Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.

Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.

It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.

In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.

Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian,, external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME, external.

At the time, she was 20 years old - making her the youngest-ever solo act to headline Glastonbury.

Aged between 24 and 32, Styles, Fender and Eilish represent the festival's youngest set of Pyramid Stage headliners since 1997.

Cher, meanwhile, will be the oldest ever act to play the legend slot - strutting through the gates of Worthy Farm at the age of 81.

The diva's appearance will come eight years after her last UK tour, and 63 years into a career that began with her ex-husband Sonny Bono, and recording sessions with Phil Spector's legendary Wrecking Crew band.

She emerged as a solo artist in the 1970s, scoring three US number ones, before switching into disco mode with Take Me Home.

In the 1980s, she became an award-winning actress and scored chart hits with FM rock staples like Turn Back Time and Just Like Jesse James.

Then in 1998, she revitalised her career with club anthem Believe, which helped to popularise the use of autotune in dance music.

Inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024, she is about to release the second volume of her memoir.

She has previously talked about retiring from live performance - but it seems the lure of Glastonbury was too tempting to turn down.

Cher will follow previous bookings in the crowd-pleasing legends slot including Sir Rod Stewart, Shania Twain, Diana Ross and Kylie Minogue.

More details about the 2027 line-up will be revealed in the New Year. Eavis has previously dismissed rumours that Madonna and Oasis will feature on the bill.

EntertainmentTab.title: Star Wars actor Osian Morgan 'thrilled' to voice the Welsh Luke Skywalker
EntertainmentTab.text:
Voicing Luke Skywalker in the Welsh-language version of Star Wars was a "dream job" according to actor Osian Morgan.

The Cardiff-born actor said he loved the film series as a child and playing one of the lead roles was "very exciting".

Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd - based on the original 1977 film Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope - was given its first showing at a red-carpet event in Cardiff on Thursday.

The dubbed Welsh version, featuring actors Matthew Rhys and Rhys Ifans, will be broadcast publicly for the first time by S4C on Christmas Day.

Almost half a century since A New Hope was first released, the sci-fi universe created by George Lucas remains one of the biggest film franchises of all time.

It has been translated into over 50 languages, with Welsh becoming its most recent.

"It feels very exciting, it's thrilling," said Morgan, who has previously starred in Welsh language soap opera Pobol y Cwm and in BBC drama Waterloo Road.

His family attended the first screening of Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd, and Morgan admitted his youngest brother had never seen any of the films before.

"Shout out to him because the first time he gets to see it in Welsh is great," he said.

Mark Lewis Jones, who voices the dark lord Darth Vader, said on the red carpet it was "nice to record the voice but not have the make-up" and joked that "the Rhosllanerchrugog accent lends itself to the dark side".

Llyr Ifans, who plays C-3PO, said he hoped the film was successful and that more Welsh-language versions would follow.

"C-3PO seems to be in all of them," he said.

"I'm quite confident it will go down well and there will be a lot of happy Welsh-speaking parents on Christmas Day."

Ifans said he been a fan of the Star Wars films since childhood, and getting invited to play the character was "surreal".

"When I first got the email through I thought 'wow, this is a bit weird doing Star Wars in Welsh' but playing C-3PO, one of the iconic parts, you can't say no, can you really?"

C-3PO is said to be fluent in six million forms of communication and Ifans said it was now one more.

The Welsh-language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August, with Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan saying the franchise was keen to expand its horizons.

"As someone who was born and raised in Wales, seeing the audience reaction to iconic Star Wars moments retold in the Welsh language was a moment of great pride," she said.

S4C chief executive Geraint Evans added that working with "one of the most iconic and influential film franchises of all time is a tremendous honour".

"It is a unique opportunity to introduce the Welsh language to new audiences around the world, while showcasing Wales and its exceptional creative talent on a global stage," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page reveals 'awful' comments from male actor
EntertainmentTab.text:
Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.

The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.

"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.

Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.

Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".

"And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."

EntertainmentTab.title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
EntertainmentTab.text:
Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members

Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.

The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.

Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.

But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.

He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".

Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.

The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.

In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.

The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.

In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.

The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.

Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.

In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".

WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.

Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.

He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
EntertainmentTab.text:
In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.”

Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold.

The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of these (mostly) Palestinian artists also weaves a traumatic national history into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interlinked world in which we now live.

It is one lesson of their work that to live in exile is to be waiting. On the floor beside Fattal’s monument stands the suitcase that Hazem Harb carried out of Gaza in 2006; above it are two framed photocollages alluding to the international airport that was bulldozed by the IDF four years earlier. These artefacts beg the question of when, and if, the artist will be able to return to his home, and who will make that decision. That powerlessness and apprehension is etched into the faces of the people photographed by Rula Halawani at Palestinian checkpoints.

Tarek Al-Ghoussein never set foot in his own country. Born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents, he explored his fragmented identity in a troubling series of photographs displayed here on glowing lightboxes. The self in these self-portraits emerges in the unsettling combination of symbols (notably the black-and-white keffiyeh that covers his face) with settings (an airport runway, a target range, an abattoir). A picture of the artist, who died in 2022, looking out to sea like Caspar David Friedrich’s wanderer does not inspire awe at the grandeur of the native landscape so much as indignation at the subject’s separation from his own.

Those who cannot see their own homeland are forced to invent it, which might be why so many storytellers are exiles. Also born in the Gulf to Palestinian émigrés, Basma Al-Sharif set out to tell a conventional “love story” set in the Levant. But she got caught up in the networks of nationalism and identity that must govern her characters’ lives, and so her elaborate fiction instead bears witness – through video, photographs, and botanical drawings of “native” and “invasive” species – to the impossibility of disentangling any individual story from the social and political conditions that frame it. That fact is especially obvious in this charged historical context. It reminds us that to make art for its own sake is a privilege of the few, made possible by injustices that are no less real for being out of sight.

Not only is it a cliche that Palestine is the “land of milk and honey”, as the ironic title of an installation furnished with artificial grass and potted plants suggests, but it is no longer true. At least not in the telling of Khalil Rabah, whose sardonic paintings of road signs indicating bodies of water in parched landscapes offer a reminder that destruction of the natural environment is a strategy of occupation going back at least as far as the Romans (“they make it a desert and call it peace” was Tacitus’s phrase originally). The images of rain, drought, water and sea that recur through the show – and in a neighbouring exhibition of paintings by the Gazan art collective Eltiqa – are not merely poetic metaphors.

For all that this is a show presenting Palestinian histories from Palestinian perspectives, using works from the collection of a UAE-based foundation with a longstanding commitment to that cause, it is only in giving three rooms to the work of Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara that it slips into agitprop. That these painted reliefs of Palestinian heroes battling imperialist dogs are propaganda does not automatically disqualify them as art – think of John Heartfield’s anti-Nazi photocollages, El Lissitzky’s revolutionary posters, or the vast majority of historical paintings of state leaders and religious icons – but the show would have been better served by a smaller selection, especially if that made space for artists such as Emily Jacir and Mona Hatoum, both of whom are represented in the collection of the Sharjah Art Foundation but surprisingly absent here.

Yet Abdul Hay’s work does serve to connect the Palestinian story to anti-imperialist struggles from Pinochet’s Chile to apartheid-era South Africa. Most notable in the context of this ex-military hospital is a painting commemorating the hunger strikers who died in the Maze in 1981, affirming a link between Irish republicanism and Palestinian independence that endures to this day and informs (and makes possible) such a forthright exhibition in a state-funded institution. Here is a final reminder that art can never entirely be separated from the systems – political, economic, migratory – that produce the societies in which we live, at least until we achieve a collective utopia. Until that time arrives, this timely spotlight on Palestinian artists meets the function ascribed to art by the great critic John Berger, who was born 100 years ago this month: to show the future “what the past has suffered” and thereby to serve as “a meeting place for the invisible, the irreducible, and the enduring”.
